meta.title: Oil, gas and offshore, 18 days of posts
meta.subject: oil and gas policy in Texas — the Railroad Commission and its races, severance taxes and the Economic Stabilization Fund, offshore leasing and drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, the General Land Office, flaring and produced water rules, orphan wells and plugging, pipelines and eminent domain, and the industry's role in state politics
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 18, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas oil, gas and offshore, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Radical Rosenthal culture-war attacks
lanes.description: Casts the Democratic Railroad Commission candidate as a woke, radical or morally unfit figure, using social media follows, Satanic Temple prayer remarks, Pride comments, and 'communist' or 'creepy' labels, and urges voters to keep him off the Commission.

lanes.label: Industry money, capture, conflicts of interest
lanes.description: Argues that oil and gas money, donors, and insider loyalties shape who runs the Railroad Commission and Texas politics, or points to conflicts of interest and spending on the Commission and its contracts.

lanes.label: Engineer versus insider qualifications
lanes.description: Argues over who is qualified to regulate the industry, with one side saying an engineer with hands-on experience is needed and the other saying he lacks petroleum or Commission experience or is an environmental puppet.

lanes.label: Produced water, flaring, environmental harm
lanes.description: Treats produced water, flaring and wastewater as the industry's biggest environmental and resource question, whether as a polluter problem to regulate or as a reuse opportunity for data centers and water supply.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability
lanes.description: Presents Texas oil and gas as the backbone of the state and national economy, tied to energy independence, geopolitical threats, fuel prices, jobs and school funding, and opposes any 'transition' or new costs.

lanes.label: Say yes to permits, pipelines, LNG
lanes.description: Argues the Railroad Commission should keep drilling permits, pipelines, LNG and refinery projects moving and avoid red tape, fees and mandates, citing new Texas investment and takeaway capacity.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Dissident Landman
posts.text:
Vote for Bo French for the Texas Railroad Commission.  

This is a bit in the weeds for industry outsiders, but I'm going to give it a shot anyway.  

Jon Rosenthal is far too ideologically compromised to be allowed at the helm of the Railroad Commission.  Allowing him to tinker with that agency will cause serious damage to the Texas economy.

Below is just ONE of a litany of destructive policies Rosenthal openly wants to pass.  We don't even know yet which policies he'll push that are too radical for him to say out loud before an election.

On to the policy:

Rosenthal wants to end routine flaring and venting of gas across Texas except in narrow emergencies, with continuous monitoring, strict capture rules, with extractive penalties for operators who don’t comply. That policy will damage the oil and gas industry.

That's not debatable.  It's a fact.

Flaring in the Permian isn’t some optional habit. Most of those wells are drilled for oil. The gas that comes with it is a byproduct, and a lot of the time there’s nowhere for it to go, except for flaring.

Gathering lines, compressors, plants, and the big pipelines to the Gulf Coast don’t appear the day a well is completed. They take years and serious money. New pads, remote leases, plant turnarounds, or just plain capacity limits mean the gas has to be handled on the spot. Texas rules already push operators to burn it in a flare rather than vent it raw, and the Railroad Commission hands out temporary exceptions under Rule 32 for exactly these cases. When the pipes are full, Waha prices (spot prices at the hub near Pecos) routinely drop to nothing or go negative. Operators have had to PAY to get rid of the gas just so they can keep producing oil. The flare is what lets the well stay online while midstream catches up.

Shut that option down except for narrow emergencies and the choices get ugly fast. No place to put the gas and no permit to flare it means you shut the well in. Oil stops. Royalty checks stop. Severance taxes stop. The cash that was going to drill the next location dries up. Marginal wells that penciled with a temporary flare become stranded. Smaller operators who can’t write a check for miles of new line and compression feel it first; even the bigger ones slow down because they have to overbuild pipe ahead of every pad or risk curtailments. Those costs don’t vanish. They show up as fewer wells, less production, and higher prices down the line for everything that runs on those barrels.

I’ve watched this for years on the land side. The pipes eventually get built when the economics support them. A hard ban doesn’t speed that up. It will idle wells, leave reserves in the ground, and pull money out of the pockets of landowners, counties, and the state at a time when commodity prices are skyrocketing.

We need responsible energy policies that take the realities of the industry into consideration.  Like it or hate it, the world runs on oil.  We need it and we do it cleaner and more safely than the foreign producers we would otherwise have to buy from.

By now, we should all have a CRYSTAL CLEAR understanding of how destructive hard left energy policies are.  For perspective, ask your favorite AI to compare the difference between a gallon of gas in California and a gallon of gas in Texas.

California is an energy rich state.  The difference between CA's and TX's gas price is a CHOICE that's rooted in politics and irresponsible energy policy. 

#BoFrench #TexasRRC #EnergyFirst #TexasStrong

South Korea and the US just announced a $22.3 billion power plant for a Texas town of 540 people.

It will be bigger than both of Texas's nuclear plants combined.

It's called Project Star: an energy campus near Encinal in La Salle County, announced on September 30.

6.47 gigawatts of natural gas generation, built to power a 5 gigawatt data center campus next door. Excess power goes back to the ERCOT grid.

The power campus will be jointly owned by the two countries, under last year's trade deal.

Nothing is built yet. First power is expected as early as 2029, and permits and approvals still have to come through.

But the location makes sense, and it starts with what's under the ground:

In October 2008, Petrohawk announced a well in La Salle County called the STS 241 #1H. It was the discovery well that opened up the Eagle Ford Shale.

Lewis Energy, which has worked in La Salle County for decades, is supplying the land, the natural gas and the water.

The Governor has told data centers to bring their own generation to the grid. This one brings South Texas gas.

At peak construction, an estimated 8,400 people will work on it. That's more than 15 times the population of Encinal.

The Eagle Ford was opened up in La Salle County in 2008. Eighteen years later, the same county could turn South Texas gas into computing power.

posts.name: Owen Gregorian
posts.text:
New US plant to turn wastewater into 3,000 tons of lithium for batteries | Georgina Jedikovska, Interesting Engineering

The US has reportedly launched its first new lithium mining plant in the last five decades, which is expected to produce at least 3,000 tons of the critical mineral annually from oilfield wastewater.

The site is located in Midland, Texas. It started commercial operations in February, 2026. This marked the first time a new US lithium mining project had reached the market since the late 1960s.

Built by clean-tech firm Element3, it relies on technology from the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) to extract lithium from wastewater generated during oil and gas production.

According to ORNL, the plant’s annual production capacity is equivalent to nearly half of current US lithium output. The country currently produces approximately 5,000 to 6,000 metric tons of lithium per year. “We can produce our own starting materials, like for battery manufacturing for example,” Parans Paranthaman, PhD, a materials scientist and corporate fellow at ORNL, said.

Lithium from oilfield brines

The facility extracts lithium from produced water, a type of wastewater generated during oil and gas extraction in the Permian Basin.. Data shows that the US oil and gas industry generates approximately 25.9 billion barrels of wastewater, known as produced water or brine, each year. That amounts to roughly 1.09 trillion gallons annually, or nearly three billion gallons per day.

Although this water contains lithium, it also carries numerous other elements that must be separated before the mineral can be used in batteries. These can include dissolved and suspended salts, heavy metals, hydrocarbons, as well as radioactive materials.

Paranthaman highlighted the difficulty of separating lithium from other elements. “The feedstock contains all kinds of elements, so you need to selectively extract the element of interest with high efficiency and low cost as you scale up,” he continued.

Cl) from the wastewater before converting it into battery-grade lithium carbonate powder. This feat also reflects the work of the DOE’s Minerals to Materials Supply Chain Research Facility (METALLIC).

Launched in April 2025, the project brings together nine DOE national labs across four research centers. Its aim is to boost mineral extraction, separation, refining as well as manufacturing technologies. Element3 licensed ORNL’s lithium recovery technology in 2024. The process has since moved from research to commercial use.

Securing domestic lithium supplies

According to ORNL, the technology could reduce reliance on overseas processing and create a domestic source of materials necessary for battery production. “You need lithium hydroxide or lithium carbonate, and we are producing those chemicals at the Texas site,” Paranthaman said.

He added that this could make it possible for the US to produce its own lithium. “This is a domestic supply chain,” he continued. For reference, the US produces less than one percent of the world’s lithium and relies heavily on imports.

The nation’s domestic output is estimated at up to 4,000 metric tons per year. Yet, most of the imported lithium comes from countries such as Chile and Argentina, which together account for 95 percent of the US lithium imports.

“We want to optimize material processing methods, reduce environmental impact and recover more value from materials,” Paranthaman noted in a press statement.

METALLIC allows companies and universities to test their technologies ahead of their commercial deployment. The initiative could strengthen US critical mineral supply chains. “The success of Element3 is what METALLIC’s innovation ecosystem aims to emulate with keystone companies,” Paranthaman concluded.

posts.text:
Texas oilfield wastewater could help cool data centers without draining freshwater | Muskanbhatia, Interesting Engineering

Can waste water from the oil and energy industry quench the thirst of data centers? Researchers at The University of Texas in Austin are betting it can.

They suggest that established desalination technologies could allow data centers to use salty or contaminated water to meet their cooling needs, reducing their reliance on freshwater.

Although there are various ways to separate salt from water, researchers said reverse osmosis, which uses pressure to push water through a semipermeable membrane, is more energy-efficient. However, the technology has one drawback: it struggles to treat water saltier than seawater.

Heating water into vapor and then condensing it back into freshwater is another viable solution, but this method requires more energy.

Turning wastewater into coolant

According to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day. The waste water generated by certain oil fields in Texas is over thousand fold higher than this amount.

Data centers can become more efficient in their water usage if they reduce stress on local water resources without drastically increasing costs or overall energy demand, according to a recently published study in Water Research.

“We’re not waiting for a futuristic technology to come along and solve this problem for us,” said Vaibhav Bahadur, who is a professor at the University’s Cockrell School of Engineering’s Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering and is one of the leaders of the research.

Bahudur noted that though the desalinations methods are available but they incur a cost. These costs, however, will be a small fraction of a data center’s total energy footprint when compared even with the most energy-intensive water treatment.

Texas oilfields offer alternatives

He proposed turning attention to the Permian Basin. This geological region in West Texas generates approximately 8 billion gallons of produced water per day during oil and gas extraction.

The researcher said this water could be put to better use instead of being transported elsewhere for disposal, where it could pose long-term risks.

“The Permian (Basin) puts out 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools per day, and right now this water is transported over long distances and injected underground. This is problematic in many ways including the risk of seismic activity,” Bahadur said. “We’re also running out of space to bury that water, by as early as 2030. We need to find a way to use it, and cleaning it up for data centers is a great way to do that.”

The research finding becomes significant given that only less than 4 percent of Earth’s water is freshwater, and only a fraction of it, just 0.5 percent, is accessible and safe for human consumption. Additionally, by 2028, water consumption by data centers is expected to reach approximately 33 billion gallons, filling nearly 50,000 Olympic-sized pools, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

posts.text:
"Conflict of interest" Interesting phrase, isn't it? 🤠

Especially when people are so QUICK to question everyone else's motives.

Or perhaps the more interesting words are MONEY, BUSINESS, LOYALTY and REVENGE.

Welcome to West Texas.

If you've watched Taylor Sheridan's LANDMAN, starring Billy Bob Thornton, you'll appreciate why I find the politics of the oil business, fascinating (and want nothing to do with it).

In smaller sized places like Midland, Texas, business relationships can span generations. Families know families. Competitors become partners. Partners become adversaries. And yesterday's commercial dispute can cast a long shadow over tomorrow's relationships. Reminds me the birthplace of Vendettas, ancient Greece (Crete and Mani).

Crete has a deep-rooted vendetta tradition, although “birthplace” is more poetic than historically precise. Blood feuds arose in multiple societies, including Crete and Mani (located South of Sparta).

The distinctly Cretan mechanism was collective honour: an injury to one person could be treated as an injury to the entire family. Responsibility, and the OBLIGATION to retaliate, could then pass across generations, with families alternating between victim and perpetrator. Anthropological research on mountainous Crete documents precisely that pattern.

Now, here's something worth examining.

Meet the Slocums.

In February 2022, Texas news outlets reported that Tom Slocum Jr., then running for Texas Railroad Commissioner, was a cousin of John Harvey Slocum, who was running for Texas House District 14.

Interesting family connection.

Now consider the historical court records involving VON Directional Services and VON Energy Services.

Federal litigation filed in April 2017 by Scientific Drilling International named both companies as defendants.

The docket subsequently recorded bankruptcy notices involving VON Directional in July 2018 and VON Energy in February 2019.

Another federal case identifies a John H. Slocum in litigation involving the VON businesses.

These are matters of public record.

And then we have Tom Slocum, who has been particularly vocal in his criticism of Greg McCabe, a central figure in the Next Bridge Hydrocarbons and $MMTLP story.

Here's where the conversation becomes educational.

When evaluating someone's commentary about a business dispute, I believe there are three important questions:

1. FOLLOW THE MONEY.
Who stands to gain or lose financially from the outcome?

2. FOLLOW THE RELATIONSHIPS.
Are there previous business dealings, professional associations, family connections or financial interests that might provide useful context?

3. FOLLOW THE HISTORY.
Have the parties previously been involved in commercial disputes, litigation or failed ventures?

These questions do not presume wrongdoing.

They help distinguish independent analysis from commentary/trolls/opinions that might be influenced by interests the audience cannot see.

And there's a fourth question that's sometimes overlooked:

WHEN DOES A COMMERCIAL DISAGREEMENT BECOME PERSONAL?

Anyone who has spent time building businesses knows that money and reputation can provoke powerful emotions.

A failed deal can destroy a friendship. A lawsuit can leave lasting resentment. A bankruptcy can affect an entire network of business relationships.

Occasionally, business disagreements can become personal vendettas, especially in smaller places like Sicily, Crete, Sparta, Midland Texas.

That doesn't establish that this has happened here. But it is precisely why understanding the historical relationships matters.

So, Tom, I have just a couple straightforward questions:

1. Are there any historical business dealings, financial interests or personal relationships relevant to your criticism of Greg McCabe that shareholders should understand?

2. Can we establish the complete history between the relevant businesses and individuals, rather than relying on selectively presented narratives? Specifically, is Mr J H Slocum your cousin (1st or other degree) by blood? Are you aware if G McCabe was one of the 99+ creditors that formed the committee to take Mr Slocum down? 

Remember, i am not passing judgement here, just want to understand where you are all coming from. 

If the answer and the data reveals no "conflict of interest", excellent! I will be more than happy to take this post down and issue an apology when requested. 

THE BIGGER LESSON FOR SHAREHOLDERS:

Don't confuse opinions with credibility.
Don't mistake confidence for independence.

And never assume that the loudest person in the room is necessarily the one with the least at stake.

Investigate the incentives. Examine the documents. Understand the relationships.

Because sometimes the most important part of a story isn't what somebody is saying.

It's what they may have experienced LONG before they started saying it.

As for West Texas?

They've already made a television series about what happens when oil, money, family, POLITICS and business rivalries collide.

It's called LANDMAN.

And sometimes the real business world has more complicated relationships than anything Hollywood could ever write. 🍿

I'll leave just three public records and sources below (there is plenty more for those who want to look further).

1.https://t.co/bSrflPd8zB

2. KBTX reported during the 2022 Texas Railroad Commission Republican primary that “Tom Slocum, Jr.” was an engineering consultant and added that he was “the cousin of John Harvey Slocum,” who at the time was running for Texas House District 14. https://t.co/4FgkjoCSfd

3. the bankruptcy chronology is quite specific. VON Directional Services filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition on July 9, 2018 in the Southern District of Texas, case 18-33794. It was converted to Chapter 7 on September 25, 2018 after the unsecured creditors' committee sought appointment of a Chapter 11 trustee and the parties instead agreed to conversion. Public docket summaries show the case as an asset case and record its eventual termination in April 2025: https://t.co/KOGij8t2iv
